source: original; stimulus table compiled from the United States Census Bureau, decennial censuses 1950-1980

stimulus.source_note: Table compiled from the United States Census Bureau, decennial censuses 1950-1980, and the Census Bureau's urban population series.
stimulus.text:
Population of the United States (United States Census Bureau, decennial censuses; urban share from the Census Bureau):

| Census | Population | Growth since last census | Living in urban areas |
| 1950 | 151.3 million | 14.5% | 64.0% |
| 1960 | 179.3 million | 18.5% | 69.9% |
| 1970 | 203.2 million | 13.3% | 73.6% |
| 1980 | 226.5 million | 11.5% | 73.7% |

stem: What does the table show about where Americans lived?

options.text: The urban share fell steadily from 1950 to 1980 without a break.
options.misconception: The urban column rises from 64.0 percent in 1950 to 73.7 percent in 1980.

options.text: The urban share rose sharply from 1950 to 1970, then almost stopped rising.
Almost no Americans at all lived in urban areas by the year 1980.
options.misconception: The urban column reads 73.7 percent in 1980, nearly three in four Americans.

options.text: The urban share doubled between the years 1970 and 1980 alone.
options.misconception: The urban column moves only from 73.6 percent to 73.7 percent between 1970 and 1980.

rationales.A: The urban column rises from 64.0 percent in 1950 to 73.7 percent in 1980.
rationales.B: The urban share climbs from 64.0 percent to 73.6 percent by 1970, then moves only to 73.7 percent by 1980.
rationales.C: The urban column reads 73.7 percent in 1980, nearly three in four Americans.
rationales.D: The urban column moves only from 73.6 percent to 73.7 percent between 1970 and 1980.
rationales.general:
1. Read the urban column: 64.0, 69.9, 73.6, 73.7 percent.
2. The jumps are large from 1950 to 1960 and from 1960 to 1970, then tiny from 1970 to 1980.
3. A rise that slows to almost nothing is a change in pace, not a reversal.
4. The population column kept growing, so the leveling off is about where people lived, not how many there were.
Remember: A column can keep rising while its pace of rise falls to nearly zero.
